endorsements.quote: Second, governance frameworks will need to be established to guide technology adoption.
Data capture and storage will need to be standardized, and healthcare staff will need to be trained on how to use new AI tools while minimizing risks like hallucination.

Furthermore, EHR and workflow integration will be a necessity to ensure that increasing digital tools do not simultaneously increase the workload associated with context switching and logging into multiple platforms.

unlisted_practices: Redesign workflows to eliminate or automate lower-value activities before introducing new AI-generated insights.
Design AI patient-preference tools to synthesize and relay patient preferences back to the primary care physician to avoid creating information silos.
Calibrate AI alerting systems carefully to avoid under-alerting that misses critical events.
Address digital literacy, smartphone access, and algorithmic bias gaps so AI does not further marginalize populations facing the greatest accessibility challenges.
Establish standards clarifying legal accountability between provider organizations and AI companies for erroneous AI-augmented advice or missed critical events.
Invest in infrastructure and workforce development, including standardized data capture and storage, to support AI tools.
Audit AI training data for underrepresentation.
Monitor AI tools for differential performance across populations after deployment.
Measure whether AI tools are reducing or exacerbating existing health disparities.

Include both technology specialists and clinicians in governance frameworks to set criteria for evaluating and piloting AI technologies, including clinical validity, legal and bias risks, and feasibility of integration.

screen.reason: This is a perspective piece discussing opportunities and implementation considerations for AI in patient-centered medical homes.
